sessions.title: Stalemate — The Sneaky Draw
sessions.concept: Stalemate: no legal move and NOT in check = draw
sessions.objective: Distinguish stalemate from checkmate and choose a mating move instead of accidentally stalemating.

sessions.objective: Demonstrate Level 2A mastery on novel positions to earn the Tactical Eyes milestone.

sessions.title: Deflection
sessions.concept: Deflection — forcing an enemy piece to leave a square or duty it is required to hold, then exploiting the abandoned square.
sessions.objective: Win material or force checkmate by deflecting (forcing away) an enemy piece from a square or duty it must keep — usually with a check or a capture the opponent cannot ignore.

sessions.title: Decoy & Attraction
sessions.concept: Decoy and attraction — luring an enemy piece (usually the king) onto a fatal square with a forcing check or sacrifice, then striking with a fork or mate.
sessions.objective: Use a decoy/attraction — a forcing check or sacrifice the opponent must accept — to lure an enemy piece (usually the king) onto a fatal square, setting up a fork or checkmate.

sessions.title: Removing the Defender (Full)
sessions.concept: Removing the defender — eliminating the enemy piece that guards a key target square or mating square, then capturing the undefended target or delivering mate.
sessions.objective: Plan and execute the removal of a defender to win material or mate.

sessions.title: Overloading
sessions.concept: Overloading — exploiting an enemy piece burdened with two or more defensive duties by attacking one duty with a forcing move so the other target collapses.
sessions.objective: Identify an overloaded enemy piece — a defender burdened with two or more duties — and exploit it with a forcing move so that, when it answers one threat, the other target falls.

sessions.title: Interference & In-Between Moves
sessions.concept: The in-between move (zwischenzug) — inserting a forcing move, usually a check or a larger threat, BEFORE the expected reply or recapture, so the opponent is forced into a worse outcome; and interference — interposing a piece to cut the line between an enemy piece and what it guards.
sessions.objective: Find the in-between move (zwischenzug) — a surprising forcing move.

sessions.objective: Solve mixed advanced-tactic problems by first IDENTIFYING which motif a position calls for — deflection, decoy, removing the defender, overloading, or the in-between move — and then executing the combination, naming the motif for each position before playing the move.

sessions.title: King and Rook versus King
sessions.concept: Checkmating a lone king with king and rook (the box method): the rook cuts the enemy king into a box, your king comes up to take the opposition, you shrink the box step by step with rook checks, and the rook mates on the edge — never stalemating.
sessions.objective: Checkmate a lone king with king and rook using the box method.

sessions.title: The Opposition
sessions.concept: The opposition in king-and-pawn-versus-king endings: kings face each other with one empty square between, and the side not to move forces the other king aside. The attacker uses it to escort the king in front of the pawn to a key square and queen (king first, not pawn first); the defender uses it to block and draw; the rook-pawn corner is the drawn exception.
sessions.objective: Use the opposition in king-and-pawn-versus-king endings.

sessions.title: Key Squares & the Square of the Pawn
sessions.concept: Two tools for deciding whether a lone king can catch a passed pawn: the rule of the square (for an unescorted pawn, draw the square whose side is the pawn's moves to promote — counting a 2nd-rank pawn from the 3rd — and the king catches it if inside the square or able to step in on its move) and key squares (when your own king escorts, lead it onto a square two ranks ahead of the pawn to queen by force).
sessions.objective: Decide whether a lone king can catch a passed pawn, using two promotion-geometry tools: the RULE OF THE SQUARE for an unescorted pawn.

sessions.title: Passed Pawns — Create & Push
sessions.concept: Passed pawns decide endings: a passed pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it or on the adjacent files, so only a king can stop it. Today's job is to RECOGNISE one and to CREATE one — by a pawn breakthrough that sacrifices to clear a lane, or by capturing away from the enemy king to make an outside passer. (The protected passer is named as a preview, and pushing the passer home is revision of S072-S073.)
sessions.objective: Recognise a passed pawn — no enemy pawn ahead of it or on either neighbouring file, so only a king can stop it — and CREATE one in two ways: the pawn BREAKTHROUGH.

sessions.title: Promotion Races
sessions.concept: A promotion race is decided by counting tempi: count how many single steps each passed pawn needs to reach the back rank — the side to move effectively counts one fewer, and queening even one move earlier wins. When the enemy can also queen, promote WITH TEMPO: a new queen that gives CHECK skewers the enemy king and the enemy queen when they share a file, rank, or diagonal, and wins the queen. If an enemy pawn blocks your runner, sacrifice a pawn to deflect it, then count the survivor home.
sessions.objective: Win a pawn race by counting tempi and promoting with tempo. Count how many single moves each passed pawn needs to reach the queening square — the side to move effectively counts one fewer, and queening even ONE move earlier wins the race.

sessions.objective: Apply THE SCAN to fundamental endgames: first NAME the endgame TYPE, then state the winning or drawing PLAN, then play it out against active resistance — so that recognising the type drives the technique. Convert basic winning endgames and hold basic drawn ones.

sessions.concept: Interleaved review of the unit's five fundamental endgames: NAME the type cold (king-and-rook mate, the opposition, the square of the pawn, passed pawns, promotion races), decide whether to convert / hold / evaluate, then execute the plan that type calls for — with no theme announced to give the answer away.

sessions.title: Control the Center
sessions.concept: The center is the four squares d4, e4, d5 and e5 — the high ground of the board. A piece in the center reaches the most squares and can swing to either wing fastest, so the first job of the opening is to fight for these squares. There are three ways to fight: OCCUPY the center with a pawn (1.e4 or 1.d4 grabs space and controls the squares beside it), DEVELOP knights and bishops so they attack central squares, and CHALLENGE an enemy pawn that lands in the center by striking it with a pawn of your own. When you must recapture, take TOWARD the center to keep a pawn in the middle.
sessions.objective: Choose opening moves that fight for the center — occupying it with pawns, aiming pieces at it, and challenging the enemy when they try to take it.

sessions.title: Develop Your Pieces
sessions.concept: Development means getting your pieces off the back rank and into the game. In the opening you have four minor pieces — two knights and two bishops — asleep at home, and the player who wakes them up fastest, on the best squares, gets the attack first. Three rules guide development: (1) Knights before bishops — a knight belongs on f3/c3 (or ...f6/...c6) where it hits the center, and that square is clear from move one, while a bishop should wait until you can see which diagonal is best. (2) Bring out a NEW piece every move — never shuffle the same piece twice or drag the queen out early to be chased. (3) Develop toward the center and castle — each piece should fight for the middle and clear the path so the king can castle to safety. A lead in development means more pieces ready to attack.
sessions.objective: Develop all four minor pieces quickly and purposefully in the opening — bringing out knights before bishops, putting each piece on a square that fights for the center, never moving the same piece twice, and finishing with castling.

sessions.title: Castle Early — King Safety
sessions.concept: King safety is the first job of the opening. While your king sits in the center on e1 (or e8), it is exposed: the moment the central files and diagonals open, enemy pieces deliver checks and the king has nowhere to hide. Castling solves this in a single move — the king jumps two squares toward a corner and a rook leaps to its other side, so the king ends up tucked behind an unbroken wall of three pawns while a rook swings toward the center. The rule of thumb is to castle EARLY, usually by about move ten, as soon as you have developed a knight and a bishop and cleared the squares between king and rook. You can castle king-side (the short castle, O-O) behind the f-, g- and h-pawns, or queen-side (the long castle, O-O-O) behind the a-, b- and c-pawns; choose the side whose pawn shield is still intact. If a piece still blocks the path, first develop that last piece — then castle next move. Develop, get the king safe, THEN attack.
sessions.objective: Castle early in the opening — by about move ten — to tuck the king safely into the corner behind an intact wall of pawns and connect the rooks, recognising when castling is the right move and which side is safer to castle to.

sessions.title: Opening Don'ts
sessions.concept: Good opening play has three simple rules — take the center, develop your pieces, and castle your king to safety. "Opening Don'ts" are the three classic ways beginners break those rules, and each one hands the opponent free time. DON'T bring your queen out too early: the queen is your most valuable piece, so the moment it stands in the open the enemy develops knights and bishops that attack it, and you waste move after move running it to safety while your opponent brings out a whole army. DON'T move the same piece twice in the opening without a real reason: every move you re-touch one developed piece is a move you did NOT use to wake up a sleeping one, so you fall behind in development. DON'T grab pawns with pieces in the opening: chasing a stray pawn drags a piece offside, costs tempo, and often leaves your king stuck in the center while the opponent opens lines. The flip side is just as important: when your OPPONENT breaks a Don't, punish it — develop a piece that attacks the early queen, so you gain time for free, then finish developing and castle. Develop with purpose, one new piece at a time, and let greedy or careless opponents lose the race.
sessions.objective: Identify and avoid the three classic opening mistakes — bringing the queen out too early, moving the same piece twice, and grabbing pawns instead of developing — and know how to punish an opponent who makes them by developing a new piece with tempo.

sessions.title: The Opera Game (Model Game)
sessions.concept: The Opera Game is the most famous teaching game in chess history: in 1858 the American champion Paul Morphy, playing White against two amateurs (the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard) during a night at the opera, won in just seventeen moves by doing nothing magical — only following the opening principles you have already learned, one after another, perfectly. He took the center with 1.e4 and 3.d4. He developed a new piece almost every move — Nf3, Bc4, Nc3, Bg5 — always toward the center and always with a purpose, often hitting something so that he gained time. He castled (12.O-O-O) and in the very same move swung his rook onto the open d-file, straight at Black's uncastled king. His opponents, meanwhile, broke the rules: they left pieces at home, wasted moves, and never got their king to safety. Once every White piece was working and every Black piece was tangled up, Morphy finished with a combination — the breakthrough 13.Rxd7 to remove a defender, and the dazzling queen sacrifice 16.Qb8+!! that decoys the last guard so that 17.Rd8# is checkmate. The lesson of the Opera Game is simple and powerful: you do not need tricks to win in the opening — develop every piece, castle your king, aim at the enemy king, and the tactics will appear by themselves. Lead in development is the engine; the sacrifice is just the finish.
sessions.objective: Explain how each of Morphy's moves in the Opera Game follows an opening principle.

sessions.title: The Four Questions of Evaluation
sessions.concept: The four questions of evaluation — material, king safety, activity, pawn structure — combined into a single verdict
sessions.objective: Learn to size up a quiet position with the four questions - material, king safety, piece activity, and pawn structure - and then play the move that improves the factor that matters most, instead of hunting for a forcing tactic that isn't there.

sessions.title: Material & Imbalances
sessions.concept: Material imbalances: judging positions where the two sides hold different pieces of similar value, and who the imbalance favours.
sessions.objective: Assess non-equal material imbalances — the exchange (rook vs a minor), two minor pieces against a rook, three minors against a queen, and the bishop pair — and say which side each imbalance favours.

sessions.title: Active vs Passive Pieces
sessions.concept: Piece activity as an evaluation factor
sessions.objective: Judge whether each of your pieces is active or passive, then find the one that is doing the least and improve it with a quiet move.

sessions.title: King Safety in Evaluation
sessions.concept: King safety as an evaluation factor
sessions.objective: Learn to ask THE KING QUESTION after counting material and judging activity: whose king is safer?

sessions.title: Who Is Better?
sessions.concept: Full evaluation: a two-factor verdict followed by a quiet press
sessions.objective: Learn to give a position one full verdict and then act on it: run all four factors — material, king safety, activity, pawn structure — say who is better, and name at least TWO factors that prove it.

sessions.title: Evaluate Then Play (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: A quick four-question scan (material, king safety, activity, pawn structure) tells you who is better and which factor is decisive — and the decisive factor points straight to the move.
sessions.objective: Practise THE PLAN by pausing at a critical moment, running the four-question evaluation scan.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Evaluation
sessions.concept: THE PLAN in evaluation: a quick four-question scan (material, king safety, activity, pawn structure) tells you who is better and which factor is decisive — and the decisive factor points straight to the move. In this Unit-1 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles turn on the same factor: students must re-run the scan on every board and ask "who is better here, and why?" instead of repeating the previous answer.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency with the four evaluation questions — material, king safety, activity, and pawn structure — by applying THE PLAN to a mixed set of positions drawn from S086/S088/S089/S090.

sessions.title: Isolated Pawns
sessions.concept: The dual nature of the isolated central pawn
sessions.objective: Understand the dual nature of the isolated central pawn - why it gives its owner energy and why it becomes a permanent target - and PRACTISE the technique against it: blockade the square in front.

sessions.title: Doubled Pawns
sessions.concept: The dual nature of doubled pawns
sessions.objective: Recognise doubled pawns - two same-colour pawns on one file that can never defend each other - and play AGAINST them: blockade the square in front of the front pawn so it can never move.

sessions.title: Backward Pawns & Holes
sessions.concept: Backward pawns and the holes in front of them
sessions.objective: Identify backward pawns and the holes/weak squares they create, and play both AGAINST them (occupy the hole, attack down the half-open file, win the fixed pawn) and WITH them (stay active and look for a freeing break).

sessions.title: Passed Pawns & Protected Passers
sessions.concept: Passed pawns and protected passed pawns — what they are, why a protected passer is the strongest pawn on the board because the enemy king is chained to it, and the two ways to create one.
sessions.objective: Students will recognise a passed pawn.

sessions.title: Pawn Chains & Breaks
sessions.concept: Pawn chains and the breaks that challenge them
sessions.objective: Identify the base of a pawn chain — the back pawn no enemy pawn can defend — choose the pawn break that attacks it from a square your own pawns guard, and say what the exchange leaves behind in the structure.

sessions.title: Structure-Based Plans (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: A pawn-structure feature on the board tells you the plan, and naming the feature first makes the right move easy to find.
sessions.objective: Practise THE PLAN by reading the pawn structure, naming the feature, choosing the plan it suggests, and playing the structural move in guided game-like positions drawn from the four Unit-2 features: isolated pawns, doubled pawns, backward pawns & holes, and pawn chains & breaks.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Pawn Structure
sessions.concept: THE PLAN in pawn-structure play: the structure on the board tells you the plan. An isolated or backward pawn is a fixed target — blockade the square in front of it, then attack it; doubled pawns are a weakness to blockade AND a half-open file for the other side to seize; a passed pawn wants to be guarded by another pawn, because a protected passer needs no piece to babysit it; a pawn chain is broken at its base. In this Unit-2 review the positions are interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share the same feature, and almost every answer is a QUIET move — students must re-read every board and ask "what is the structure here, and what plan does it demand?" instead of hunting for a tactic or repeating the previous answer.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency across the five Unit-2 pawn-structure features.

sessions.title: Rooks on Open Files
sessions.concept: Placing rooks on open and half-open files
sessions.objective: Identify open and half-open files and place rooks on them with purpose, using a rook's long-range power on an open file to win material or deliver mate.

sessions.title: Rooks on the 7th Rank
sessions.concept: The power of a rook (or pair) on the 7th rank
sessions.objective: Understand why the 7th rank is a rook's most powerful outpost, and use a rook (or a pair of doubled rooks) on the 7th to win material or deliver mate.

sessions.title: Knight Outposts
sessions.concept: Establishing knights on protected, unattackable outpost squares
sessions.objective: Recognise a knight outpost — an advanced square protected by your pawn and safe from any enemy pawn — and place a knight on it to dominate, winning material or delivering mate.

sessions.title: Good Bishop vs Bad Bishop
sessions.concept: Bishop quality relative to one's own pawn chains
sessions.objective: Tell a good bishop from a bad one by checking which colour your OWN pawns stand on, and improve a bad bishop in one quiet move by rerouting it onto a diagonal your pawns do not block.

sessions.title: The Bishop Pair
sessions.concept: The bishop pair as an activity weapon in open play
sessions.objective: Understand why two bishops outgun a bishop and a knight in open positions, and learn the quiet, no-capture habit of swinging each bishop onto a long open diagonal so BOTH bishops work together.

sessions.title: Improve Your Worst Piece (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: THE PLAN: in any position, scan all your pieces, find the worst-placed one, and make the move that gives it the best job right now.
sessions.objective: In this guided practice session, students synthesize everything they have learned in Unit 3 by applying THE PLAN: scan all your pieces, identify the one doing the least work, and give it a better job.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Piece Placement
sessions.concept: THE PLAN in piece placement: every piece has a dream square, and the position tells you which piece to improve and where. In this Unit-3 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles turn on the same placement tool: students must ask "which piece wants a better square here, and where?" on every board — a rook craving an open file or the 7th rank, a knight hunting an outpost, a good bishop wanting an open diagonal, or the bishop pair looking to rake the board — instead of repeating the previous answer.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency with the piece-placement toolkit — rooks on open files, rooks on the 7th rank, knight outposts, the good bishop, and the bishop pair — by applying THE PLAN to a mixed set of positions drawn from S100/S101/S102/S103/S104.

sessions.title: Level 3A Checkpoint: The Thinking Player
sessions.concept: Assessment of Level 3A evaluation, pawn structure, and piece placement on novel positions
sessions.objective: Demonstrate Level 3A mastery on novel positions by judging each board through the three lenses (evaluation, pawn structure, piece placement) and playing the move that presses the advantage — earning The Thinking Player milestone.

sessions.title: What Is a Plan?
sessions.concept: What a plan is — naming the enemy's weakest target, choosing a method to attack it, and playing the purposeful move that carries the method out
sessions.objective: Students learn that a plan is a target plus a method plus the move that carries it out; given a position, they name the weakest enemy point, choose how to attack it, and play the purposeful move.

sessions.title: Improving Your Worst Piece
sessions.concept: Systematically improving your least active piece
sessions.objective: Use the SPOT → FIND → PLAY habit to identify the least active piece, choose its best square, and play the move that upgrades it — then turn that improved piece into a decisive tactic or a won endgame.

sessions.title: Prophylaxis — Stop Their Idea
sessions.concept: Prophylaxis (from the Greek for 'to guard beforehand') is the habit of asking 'What does my opponent want to do?' before deciding your own move. Strong players do not chase their own ideas in a vacuum — they constantly read the other side's intentions and play moves that neutralise those intentions, ideally before the threat is even fully formed. Prophylaxis is not passive defence; it is efficient play. A single well-timed preventive move costs almost no time yet eliminates an entire plan of counterplay, freeing you to pursue your own goals without interruption. There are three tools of prevention, and the position tells you which to reach for: (1) REMOVE THE ATTACKER — capture or drive away the piece that creates the threat, killing it at the source; (2) REPOSITION or OVER-GUARD — move the threatened piece out of reach, or add a defender / cover the key square so the threat no longer bites; and (3) the IN-BETWEEN counter — when your own resources are faster, answer a threat with an even bigger threat instead of meekly defending. In every position today the opponent has just made a threatening move, and your job is to find the one reply that stops their idea cold — a reply that, checked by the engine, is also the objectively best move on the board.
sessions.objective: Before choosing a move, identify the opponent's threat or plan, and play the prophylactic move that prevents it — removing the attacker, repositioning the target, or answering with a stronger in-between blow — proven to be the position's clear best move.

sessions.title: Creating & Using Weaknesses
sessions.concept: Creating and using weaknesses — spotting an enemy target that cannot defend itself and pressing it, switching to a second when the first is held
sessions.objective: Students identify a concrete enemy weakness — a loose, trapped, or pinned piece, a weak rank, or an exposed king — and play the move that exploits it, understanding that when one target is held they must create or switch to a second.

sessions.title: Converting a Material Advantage
sessions.concept: One of the most important — and most often neglected — skills in chess is knowing what to do once you are already winning. The answer, taught by the great champions since Jose Raul Capablanca in the early twentieth century, is deceptively simple: when you are ahead in material, trade pieces and simplify. Every even exchange of pieces removes one of the opponent's resources. Their bishops, knights, and rooks are the tools they need to create counterplay, complicate the position, and confuse you. Each time you swap one off the board, their chances shrink and your extra material becomes relatively more powerful — because there are fewer pieces left to fight your advantage. Crucially, you must trade pieces but keep your pawns: pawns are your endgame currency. In a simplified position, an extra pawn marches down the board and queens; an extra piece with nothing to do in a crowded position can feel invisible. When the opponent's king is stuck in the centre on top of everything else, the resulting endgame after simplification is almost always an easy technical win — the king becomes a liability rather than an asset. This is called conversion technique, and it is a mark of the truly strategic player.
sessions.objective: Students will learn to convert a material advantage: trade pieces (not pawns) to simplify into a clearly won ending, then use king activity, the opposition, passed pawns and breakthroughs to promote and finish the game.

sessions.title: Plan & Play (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: THE PLAN is the master skill that ties every other strategic tool together. A strong player does not drift from move to move hoping something good happens; they pause, survey the whole board, and choose a specific goal. But choosing a goal is only step one — the real discipline is stating it in a single, honest sentence before touching a piece, then following through on it even when the opponent makes it inconvenient. In this session, THE PLAN functions as an umbrella: underneath it live all four tools students have studied in Unit 4. At any given moment the position will call for one (or sometimes two) of those tools, and the planner's job is to read the position correctly — Is my worst piece a rook stuck on a closed file? Then improve it. Is my opponent about to activate a dangerous piece? Then stop it first. Am I holding one weakness but the opponent is defending it easily? Then open a second front. Am I up material with the queens off? Then trade pieces and march pawns. Stating the plan aloud — to a partner, a coach, or even to themselves — builds the metacognitive habit that separates strategic players from reactive ones. Adjusting the plan is not a failure; it is proof that the student is reading the new position honestly rather than clinging to a plan the board has already refuted.
sessions.objective: Students synthesize all four Unit 4 planning tools — improving the worst piece, prophylaxis, the principle of two weaknesses, and converting a material advantage — by practicing THE PLAN thinking routine in a live guided game.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Planning
sessions.concept: THE PLAN in the middlegame and the endgame: the position on the board tells you which planning tool to reach for. Your own passive piece is a candidate to ACTIVATE onto its best square; a hole or a straggler is a TARGET to name and occupy; the opponent's idea is something to PREVENT before you push your own; a weakness that cannot be defended by a pawn is one half of the two-weakness plan; and a position you are already winning asks for CONVERSION technique instead of a fresh attack. In this Unit-4 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share the same tool — students must re-read every board and ask "what does THIS position need?" instead of repeating the previous answer. The middlegame boards are White to move and the conversion boards are Black to move, so colour changes with every puzzle too.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency across the five Unit-4 planning tools.

sessions.title: Three-Move Combinations
sessions.concept: forced three-move combination
sessions.objective: Students will calculate and execute forced three-move combinations by mapping every check and forced reply in the full line to mate before committing to move one.

sessions.title: The Greek Gift Sacrifice
sessions.concept: the Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+)
sessions.objective: Students will recognise the conditions for a sound Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) and execute the forcing three-move attack — Bxh7+, Ng5+, Qh5 — against the castled king with calculation and confidence.

sessions.title: Sacrificing for an Attack
sessions.concept: sacrificing material for a decisive attack
sessions.objective: Students will judge whether an attacking sacrifice is justified by calculating a forcing line all the way to a concrete win, and will execute several types of attacking sacrifice with confidence.

sessions.title: Defensive Tactics & Stalemate Tricks
sessions.concept: The saving capture (liquidation into insufficient material): capturing the opponent's last dangerous piece so that neither side has enough material to force checkmate, turning a lost game into an immediate draw.
sessions.objective: Students will identify and execute the saving capture — eliminating the opponent's last winning piece to reach a drawn insufficient-material ending — as a concrete defensive resource when facing a lost position.

sessions.title: Perpetual Check & Fortress
sessions.concept: Forced perpetual check: a returning loop of two consecutive checks where each forces the king's only legal reply, returning the position to its start; doubling the loop produces threefold repetition and an automatic draw.
sessions.objective: Students will identify and execute forced perpetual check — a returning loop of checks where every attacker reply is the only legal move, producing threefold repetition — to save a lost position, and understand the fortress as an alternative structural draw.

sessions.title: A Brilliant Attack (Model Game)
sessions.concept: The Immortal Game is the most famous attacking game ever played. In 1851, during a break in a London tournament, Adolf Anderssen (White) beat Lionel Kieseritzky in a friendly game so dazzling that it was nicknamed 'immortal'. Anderssen opened with the King's Gambit (1.e4 e5 2.f4), offering a pawn to rip open the centre and aim at Black's king. Black grabbed the pawn and then went hunting with the queen (3...Qh4+), winning a little material but developing almost nothing. While Black chased pawns and shuffled the same queen and knight around, Anderssen poured pieces into the game and built a battery on the g-file. When everything was aimed at the enemy king, the fireworks began. Anderssen did not count material — he counted DEFENDERS. He let a bishop go, then played 18.Bd6!!, a quiet-looking move that offers BOTH rooks just to block the black bishop's retreat and choke the king's escape squares. Black took both rooks and even checked with the queen, but it did not matter: 21.Nxg7+ dragged the king out, and 22.Qf6+!! gave up the queen to decoy the last defender, so that 23.Be7# was checkmate — delivered by three minor pieces while Black had a queen, a rook, and a bishop sitting uselessly on the other side of the board. The lesson is the biggest idea in attacking chess: material does not defend a king — pieces do. If you are far ahead in development and every piece is aimed at the enemy king, look for the forcing move that removes the last defender, and be willing to give up material to land it.
sessions.objective: Replay Anderssen's 'Immortal Game' and explain how a huge lead in development lets White give up a bishop, both rooks, and finally the queen.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Advanced Tactics & Sacrifice
sessions.concept: Win-or-Save recognition: the first diagnostic question in any mixed position is 'Am I attacking for mate or defending for a draw?' — this master switch routes you to the correct Unit 5 toolkit without wasted effort.
sessions.objective: Students will demonstrate fluency across all five Unit 5 skills by first classifying each mixed position as a WIN.

sessions.title: The Lucena Position
sessions.concept: Winning the Lucena position by 'building a bridge' — putting the rook on the fourth rank so it can interpose against the defender's side checks, freeing the king to shepherd the pawn to promotion
sessions.objective: Students learn to win the Lucena position.

sessions.title: The Philidor Position
sessions.concept: Drawing the Philidor position by the third-rank defense — keeping the king in front of the pawn and the rook on the third rank in front of it, then switching to long-range checks from behind once the pawn reaches the sixth rank
sessions.objective: Students learn to draw the Philidor position.

sessions.title: Rook Activity
sessions.concept: Activating the rook in a rook endgame — the Tarrasch rule (rook behind the passed pawn) and cutting the enemy king off — so a passed pawn, escorted by the king, promotes safely
sessions.objective: Students learn to activate the rook in a rook endgame using the two golden techniques: place the rook BEHIND a passed pawn (the Tarrasch rule) so it supports the pawn's advance, and use the rook to CUT the enemy king off from the pawn.

sessions.title: Build Your Opening Repertoire
sessions.concept: An opening repertoire is the set of openings you play regularly — your personal toolkit. A good repertoire is built on IDEAS, not memorized move sequences. Every opening has a core purpose, and once you know it, you can find good moves even in positions you have never seen. The four building-block ideas are: (1) CENTER BREAK — strike the center with a pawn to d4, d5, e4, or e5, claiming space and opening lines; (2) FLANK CHALLENGE — push a pawn to c4, c5, f4, or f5 to attack the enemy's center from the side, undermining their d- or e-pawn; (3) DEVELOPING PRESSURE — bring a knight or bishop off the back rank to a square that attacks an enemy piece, putting the opponent under immediate tactical stress; (4) CENTER SUPPORT — advance a pawn so it defends a friendly pawn already in the center zone, keeping your central pawn structure solid. When you choose an opening, ask: 'What is this opening TRYING TO DO?' If the answer is clear — 'the Italian breaks with d4', 'the Colle supports d4 with c3', 'the Sicilian challenges with c5' — then you have a plan for every move, even when the game leaves the book line. A repertoire built on ideas survives deviations; a repertoire built on memorization collapses the moment the opponent plays something different.
sessions.objective: Choose a White opening and Black answers based on their core ideas — center breaks, flank challenges, developing pressure, and center support — so every move in the opening has a clear purpose.

sessions.title: Play Your Repertoire (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Practice transforms knowledge into habit. In S125, you learned the four building-block ideas behind every opening plan — center break, flank challenge, developing pressure, and center support. In this practice session, you revisit each idea on the same openings so that recognition becomes automatic. The goal is not to learn something new; it is to make what you already know faster, more confident, and more reliable under game conditions. Spaced repetition — revisiting an idea after a short gap — is one of the most powerful learning techniques in cognitive science. Each time you encounter the same idea in the same opening, the neural pathway gets stronger and retrieval gets quicker. By the end of this session, naming the core idea of the Italian, Caro-Kann, Colle, Pirc, London, and QGD should feel like naming the color of a piece — instant and effortless.
sessions.objective: Practice naming and executing the four building-block opening ideas — center break, flank challenge, developing pressure, and center support — across familiar opening positions until recognition feels automatic and confident.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Rook Endgames & Repertoire
sessions.concept: THE PLAN in the rook endgame: the position tells you which technique to reach for. An enemy king on the queening file is a target to CUT OFF with a check; your own passed pawn wants the ROOK BEHIND it; a king stuck in front of its pawn must MARCH out to the shelter side; incoming checks are stopped by BUILDING THE BRIDGE; a pawn on the last rank is there to PROMOTE; and a lone enemy king on the edge is finished with the KING-AND-ROOK MATE. In this Unit-6 review the positions are interleaved so no two consecutive puzzles share the same technique — students must re-read every board and ask "which step of the rook-endgame method does THIS position need?" instead of repeating the previous answer.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency across the unit's rook-endgame techniques.

sessions.title: Stage 3 Comprehensive Review
sessions.concept: THE PLAN across the whole Bishop Stage: EVALUATE the position, NAME the Stage-3 idea it turns on, STATE the plan, then PLAY the move. In this comprehensive review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share a theme: students must ask "what does THIS position turn on — an evaluation factor, a structural weakness, a piece-placement tool, a plan, or an endgame technique?" on every board instead of repeating the previous answer.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate fluency across the ENTIRE Bishop Stage by applying THE PLAN to a mixed set of positions drawn from every unit.

sessions.title: Bishop Stage Final Assessment & Graduation
sessions.concept: Whole-stage assessment of the six Bishop-Stage skills on novel positions; graduation to the Rook Stage
sessions.objective: Demonstrate Bishop Stage mastery on novel positions by judging each board through the six Bishop-Stage skills and playing the move that presses the advantage — earning the Bishop Stage Graduate certificate and promotion to the Rook Stage.

sessions.title: Attacking the Castled King
sessions.concept: Attacking the castled king with open lines and more attackers
sessions.objective: Attack a king that has already castled by opening lines toward it and bringing more attackers than the defence can meet, converting the attack into decisive material or checkmate, and calculating the forcing sequence to a clear result before committing.

sessions.title: Pawn Storms
sessions.concept: Pawns are not just defenders or future queens-in-waiting — they are immediate attackers. A well-timed pawn advance or capture can shatter the enemy king's shelter, tear open files for heavy pieces, or become an unstoppable promotion threat that decides the game on its own.
sessions.objective: Students will learn to identify and execute pawn attacks in three forms — shield-smashing captures that crack open the enemy king, pawn thrusts that open files and win material, and passed-pawn storms that race to promotion.

sessions.title: Opening Lines & Sacrifices for Attack
sessions.concept: Line-opening sacrifices — giving up material to open a file, rank, or diagonal for a heavy piece to deliver checkmate through the opened line.
sessions.objective: Students will identify and execute two types of line-opening sacrifice — demolition (rook smashes shield, queen mates through opened file) and deflection (queen decoy drags guard off line, rook mates through vacated rank) — and will calculate the entire forced sequence before committing.

sessions.title: The Exchange Sacrifice
sessions.concept: The exchange sacrifice — giving a rook for a minor piece for activity or attack
sessions.objective: Recognise when giving up the exchange (a rook for a knight or bishop) is favourable, and calculate the follow-up — a tactic that wins the material back or an attack that crashes through — before committing.

sessions.title: Defensive Resources
sessions.concept: Defence is a skill, not a surrender. When the opponent attacks, calm players do not freeze or grab material blindly — they read the attack, find its spearhead, and choose the resource that meets it. This session builds a defender's toolbox and a habit for using it: the ASSESS-CHOOSE-CALCULATE loop. ASSESS the threat and name the piece delivering it; CHOOSE the resource that fits; CALCULATE the line to a safe result. There are three resources you will use directly today, and two more for your games: (1) TRADE or REMOVE THE ATTACKER — capture or exchange off the piece making the threat, killing it at the source; (2) RELOCATE and DEFEND — regroup a piece to guard the key square, over-guard it, or hem in and trap an over-extended invader; (3) COUNTERATTACK — when your own blow lands first, answer a threat with a bigger one, an in-between check or capture that seizes the initiative; (4) RETURN MATERIAL — when ahead, give some back to break the attack and simplify into a safe, winning position; and (5) the FORTRESS — a wall of pawns and pieces the enemy cannot breach, used to hold a draw from a worse position. Calculation matters most in defence, because a single overlooked check can undo everything. In every position today the opponent has just attacked, and your task is to pick the resource that meets it and calculate it out — a move that, checked by the engine, is also the objectively best move on the board.
sessions.objective: When facing an attack, identify the opponent's spearhead threat and choose the correct defensive resource — trade or remove the attacker, relocate and defend, or counterattack — then calculate the line to a safe or winning result, proven to be the position's clear best move.

sessions.title: Attack & Defense Sparring (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Sparring with both attack and defence: switch roles at the board, calculate the right method, and execute it with confidence.
sessions.objective: Practise THE CALCULATE in game-like positions where the student must switch between attacker and defender, choosing the right method — add an attacker, sacrifice the exchange, open a line, simplify by trading, prophylaxis by relocating/defending/capturing — for each situation.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Attack & Defense
sessions.concept: A fighting game has two modes, and reading which one you are in comes first: attack when the enemy king is the weaker, defend when yours is — then run THE CALCULATE to prove the plan. Attack by naming a target, opening lines with a storm or sacrifice, and calculating a forced mate; defend by assessing the threat, choosing an active resource, and calculating that your king ends up safe.
sessions.objective: Consolidate Unit-1 attacking and defensive methods by exercising JUDGMENT: on each unlabelled position, decide whether it is a moment to attack.

sessions.title: Candidate Moves
sessions.concept: Strong players do not play the first move that jumps out at them. They generate a short list of candidate moves and calculate each one to the end, then play the move they have proven is best.
sessions.objective: Students learn to pause before every move, generate two or three candidate moves from the checks, captures and threats on the board, and calculate each one to the end.

sessions.title: Calculating Forced Lines
sessions.concept: Calculating a forced line: stringing together checks, captures, and threats so that every opponent reply is forced, and following the sequence accurately to its conclusion — here, a three-move forced checkmate.
sessions.objective: Students learn to calculate a forcing sequence of checks, captures, and threats accurately to its conclusion.

sessions.title: Visualization — Three Moves Ahead
sessions.concept: Visualization is the mental skill of holding a future position clearly in your mind's eye — seeing exactly where each piece will stand after a forced sequence — so you can judge the outcome before you ever move a piece.
sessions.objective: Students learn to visualize a forced three-move sequence all the way to checkmate — picturing where every piece will land and naming the final mating square from memory — describing that future position in their mind's eye without ever touching a piece, applying THE CALCULATE.

sessions.title: Critical Moments (THE CALCULATE)
sessions.concept: A critical moment is the instant a game hangs in the balance — a forcing tactic is on the board and one routine, autopilot move can throw the whole game away — so the skill is a two-part habit: first RECOGNISE the moment from its trigger signs, then SLOW DOWN and CALCULATE the forcing line to its end before you play.
sessions.objective: Students learn to recognise a critical moment from its trigger signs, switch out of autopilot into deep calculation, and calculate a forcing line all the way to checkmate, applying THE CALCULATE from recognition through verification to the played move.

sessions.title: Blunder-Check & Opponent's Best
sessions.concept: The blunder-check is a habit you run before every move: once you have a candidate, you assume the opponent will answer with their STRONGEST reply — not the weak or hoped-for one — and you calculate your move to the end against that best defence; only if it still wins or mates do you play it, because most blunders come from calculating only the opponent's obvious answer.
sessions.objective: Students learn the blunder-check: after choosing a candidate move, pause and identify the opponent's STRONGEST reply, then calculate their move against that best defence to verify it still works before playing, applying THE CALCULATE from candidate to verified move.

sessions.title: Calculation Drills (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Calculation is a trainable habit: pick a forcing candidate, assume the opponent's best reply, calculate the whole line to checkmate in your head, verify it, then play.
sessions.objective: Practise THE CALCULATE by solving mixed mate-in-two and mate-in-three drills: for each position the student picks a candidate forcing move, assumes the opponent's strongest reply, calculates the whole line in their head to checkmate, verifies it, and only then plays.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Calculation
sessions.concept: Strong calculation is recognition plus proof: name the mating pattern you are steering toward, then run THE CALCULATE — candidate, assume the best reply, calculate the whole line to checkmate in your head, verify, and play.
sessions.objective: Review the whole Calculation & Visualization unit by solving interleaved forced-mate positions drawn from every teaching session: for each, the student names the mating pattern.

sessions.title: The Isolated Queen's Pawn
sessions.concept: isolated queen's pawn
sessions.objective: You will learn how to play both WITH and AGAINST the isolated queen's pawn.

sessions.title: Hanging Pawns
sessions.concept: hanging pawns
sessions.objective: Handle hanging pawns from both sides: as their owner, cash the space and the two half-open files they hand you.

sessions.title: The Minority Attack
sessions.concept: minority attack
sessions.objective: The student can recognise a minority-attack structure.

sessions.title: Space Advantage & Restriction
sessions.concept: space advantage
sessions.objective: Students will use a space advantage the three ways it actually pays: OCCUPY it.

sessions.title: Open vs Closed Positions
sessions.concept: open position
sessions.objective: Classify any position as open or closed using a fast structural test, and choose a fitting plan — long-range lines on open boards, knight outposts and pawn breaks on closed ones — verifying each plan with THE CALCULATE.

sessions.title: Structure-Based Middlegames (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: A pawn structure has a name, and the name comes with a plan already attached. Recognising the structure hands you the plan, the plan hands you two or three candidate moves, and THE CALCULATE tells you which one to play — so naming the structure is the fastest way to stop drifting in a middlegame.
sessions.objective: Practise THE CALCULATE on six typical pawn structures by naming the structure before anything else: the name supplies the standing plan, the plan narrows your candidate moves, and THE CALCULATE proves the best one works.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Advanced Strategy
sessions.concept: Strong strategic play begins with recognition: the pawn structure tells you which plan belongs to the position, and THE CALCULATE then proves whether your chosen move actually delivers that plan.
sessions.objective: Students consolidate the whole Advanced Strategy unit by recognising six pawn structures on sight — isolated queen's pawn, hanging pawns, minority attack, space advantage, open and closed positions — and recalling the correct plan for each, from both sides.

sessions.title: Level 4A Checkpoint: The Complete Player
sessions.concept: Level-4A assessment of structure-based middlegame play on novel positions: name the structure, recall its plan, calculate the move — the milestone into Level 4B (Complex Endgames)
sessions.objective: Demonstrate Level-4A mastery on novel positions by naming the pawn structure.

sessions.title: Bishop Endgames (Same Colour)
sessions.concept: same-coloured bishop endgame
sessions.objective: Convert winning and defend inferior same-coloured-bishop endgames by judging bishop quality, activating the king, and using THE CALCULATE to play every bishop trade and every pawn race to the very end before committing.

sessions.title: Opposite-Coloured Bishops
sessions.concept: opposite-coloured bishops
sessions.objective: Judge whether an opposite-coloured bishop ending is draw territory or winning territory, then calculate blockades and promotion races to the very end and play for the right result.

sessions.title: Knight Endgames
sessions.concept: knight endgames
sessions.objective: Handle knight endgames with confidence: calculate the pawn ending before trading knights, count race tempi against the knight's short legs, and use the fork-check as the ending's key tactical resource.

sessions.title: Bishop vs Knight
sessions.concept: Bishop's long range on open boards
sessions.objective: Students judge which minor piece the pawn structure favours and use THE CALCULATE to steer toward — or trade into — the favourable minor-piece or pawn ending.

sessions.title: Queen Endgame Basics & Q vs Pawn
sessions.concept: The checking staircase
sessions.objective: Students will win queen-versus-pawn endings against b/d/e/g-pawns with the checking staircase, hold the a/c/f/h-pawn stalemate draws, and calculate every queen trade and promotion race to the very end before playing it.

sessions.title: Practical Endgames (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Practical endgame play is a three-step decision: name the endgame family, state the goal (convert, hold, or mate), then calculate the committal move — trade, push, or promotion — to the very end before playing it.
sessions.objective: Practise correct practical decisions in complex endgames: for each unlabelled position the student names the endgame family.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Complex Endgames
sessions.concept: Complex-endgame mastery is the review ritual made automatic: name the family (it loads the right toolkit), state the goal (convert, hold, or mate), then calculate the committal move to the very end before playing it.
sessions.objective: Consolidate the Unit-4 complex-endgame toolkit by solving interleaved, unlabelled problems across all five families.

sessions.title: Time Management & the Clock
sessions.concept: The clock is a resource to budget just like material: sort every position into SNAP — play on rhythm in 10-20 seconds when it is a recapture, a known pattern, or a choice between equal safe moves — or INVEST — spend 2-5 minutes when there is a forcing sequence, a sacrifice, or an irreversible decision, and run THE CALCULATE to the very end before touching a piece — because time trouble means playing the most important moves of the game on seconds.
sessions.objective: Students learn to treat the clock as a resource to be budgeted like material, sorting every position into a quick SNAP move or a deep INVEST.

sessions.title: Notation & Tournament Rules
sessions.concept: Full algebraic notation is the written language of chess — piece letter plus destination square, x for captures, + for check, # for mate, =Q for promotion, O-O and O-O-O for castling, and a from-file or from-rank like Rgxg8 or Q6xg7 when two identical pieces can reach the same square — kept on a scoresheet in the tournament order of play the move FIRST, then write it; and it lives alongside the laws of the tournament hall: touch-move with 'I adjust', the same-hand clock press, and the etiquette of silence, polite draw offers, handshakes, and raising a hand for the arbiter.
sessions.objective: Students learn to record a complete game in full algebraic notation.

sessions.title: Handling Nerves & Pressure
sessions.concept: The four-step calming routine — BREATHE (one slow breath, drop the shoulders), LOOK (name the opponent's biggest threat out loud in your head), CALCULATE (run the candidate line to the very end exactly as THE CALCULATE taught, before the hand moves under touch-move), and TRUST (play the calculated line without flinching, even through a mid-line counter-check) — practised under a growth mindset that normalises nerves as universal (even world champions feel them), treats pressure as a signal to slow down rather than speed up, and treats every mistake as information for the next game rather than a verdict on the player.
sessions.objective: Students learn and use a four-step calming routine — BREATHE, LOOK, CALCULATE, TRUST — together with a growth mindset, so that during tense tournament moments they slow down, name the real threat, finish their forced calculation, and play it without flinching.

sessions.title: Pre-Game Preparation
sessions.concept: A repeatable six-item pre-game preparation routine, the Round-Ready checklist, in which BODY covers sleep, food and water, BAG covers set, clock, scoresheet, pen and routine card packed the night before, BOARD covers arriving early and setting up correctly with a white square bottom-right and each queen on her own colour, BRAIN covers a short timed warm-up of quick forced mates to wake pattern recognition, BEARINGS covers the pairing sheet, colour, opponent and a first move chosen in advance for each colour, and BREATH covers one slow breath before move one, so that nothing at all is left to be decided in the five minutes when a player is least able to decide well.
sessions.objective: Students will follow a six-item pre-game preparation checklist — BODY, BAG, BOARD, BRAIN, BEARINGS, BREATH — running a timed tactics warm-up of forced mates and calculating each line to its final move before touching a piece.

sessions.title: Analyze Your Own Game
sessions.concept: The post-mortem method: replay, recognise, recalculate, record
sessions.objective: Analyse one of your own games with the Four Rs and find the critical mistakes that decided it.

sessions.title: Simulated Tournament Round
sessions.concept: the full round arc under tournament conditions: pre-round checklist, clock and notation during play, signed result and post-mortem afterwards
sessions.objective: Play a full game with clock and notation under tournament rules, then post-mortem it straight away.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Tournament Skills
sessions.concept: Tournament readiness is the round ritual made automatic: settle with a breath, calculate the forced line to the very end, play it on a sensible clock budget, and record it in clean, unambiguous notation — the same routine before the clock starts, while it runs, and after you shake hands.
sessions.objective: Consolidate the Unit-5 tournament-skill toolkit using the round ritual — settle, calculate the forced line to the end, play on a sensible clock budget, and record the move in clean notation.

sessions.title: Deepening Your Repertoire
sessions.concept: opening principles
sessions.objective: Play your opening repertoire several moves deeper with correct ideas, continuing principled chess when the book runs out and proving each plan concretely with THE CALCULATE.

sessions.title: Typical Middlegame Plans from Openings
sessions.concept: pawn structure
sessions.objective: Read the pawn structure your opening leaves behind and let it tell you which wing your plan belongs on. Name that plan, then prove its breakthrough with THE CALCULATE before you commit to it.

sessions.title: Preparing Against an Opponent
sessions.concept: targeted preparation
sessions.objective: Learn to scout ONE opponent for ONE habit he repeats - the knight hop he never misses.

sessions.title: Traps & How to Avoid Them
sessions.concept: trapped piece
sessions.objective: Recognise when a piece — yours or your opponent's — has moved to a square with no safe retreat.

sessions.title: Main-Line Model Game
sessions.concept: The five stations of a model game — BOOK, JOBS, STRUCTURE, PLAN, CONVERT: read the pawn structure a main line produces, play the plan that structure hands you, and convert it by counting.
sessions.objective: Explain the opening-to-middlegame plan of a model main-line game: name where BOOK ends, read the pawn structure it produced, state the plan that structure hands you, and follow it through to a counted, converted advantage.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Opening Depth
sessions.concept: Opening depth is not more memorised moves: it is knowing which question the position is asking. Where the book ends, the four opening jobs answer it; where the pawns are uneven, the count answers it; where you know your opponent, his habit answers it; where a piece has strayed, its escape squares answer it; and where a plan has already created a weakness, only a calculated line answers it.
sessions.objective: Consolidate the Unit-6 opening-depth toolkit by recognising, without being told.

sessions.title: Stage 4 Comprehensive Review
sessions.concept: Interleaved review across all Stage 4 skills: sort the position before solving it. A mixed set removes the label that a teaching session gives away for free, so the pupil must decide from the board alone whether the answer is forcing or quiet - anything loose or any exposed king means calculate; nothing loose means name the structure and improve the worst piece - and then verify the chosen line to its end with THE CALCULATE.
sessions.objective: Solve mixed Stage 4 problems across attack, calculation and endgames by SORTING before solving.

sessions.title: Rook Stage Final Assessment & Graduation
sessions.concept: Rook Stage final assessment on novel positions across all six Stage-4 families — sort the board, name the family, play the move the skill points at; the graduation milestone into the Queen Stage
sessions.objective: Demonstrate Rook Stage mastery on novel positions by SORTING each board before solving it.

sessions.title: Imbalances
sessions.concept: the imbalance list
sessions.objective: Read out the five-item imbalance list for any quiet position, name who owns each item, and choose a move that uses the item you own.

sessions.title: Dynamic vs Static Advantages
sessions.concept: dynamic vs static advantages
sessions.objective: Sort the edges in a quiet position into the static column and the dynamic column, decide whether the dynamic edge can be turned into something permanent right now, and either spend it this move or convert it into a lasting one.

sessions.title: Prophylactic Thinking
sessions.concept: prophylactic thinking
sessions.objective: Consistently include the opponent's plan in your own decision-making: name his single sharpest idea in one sentence, then remove it with a quiet move that keeps every edge you already own.

sessions.title: Maneuvering in Closed Positions
sessions.concept: maneuvering in closed positions
sessions.objective: Improve pieces by maneuvering when the position is closed: prove the pawns are locked, find the worst piece by counting its squares, name the address it belongs on.

sessions.title: Two Weaknesses (Advanced)
sessions.concept: two weaknesses
sessions.objective: Understand why a single weakness rarely wins a game, and practise the two-front method: count the opponent's weak pawns wing by wing, check whether his defenders already match your attackers there, and.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Deep Strategy
sessions.concept: Interleaved review of advanced strategic themes: the unit's five ways of thinking — imbalances, static versus dynamic advantages, prophylaxis, maneuvering in closed positions and the two-weaknesses method — are met again in mixed order and without labels, so the pupil has to decide which one the position is asking for. The single routine that makes the choice is THE EVALUATE: list what each side owns, ask which items are permanent and which expire, choose the plan the list points at, and check the opponent's best answer before committing.
sessions.objective: Form a deep strategic plan in a mixed position by running one routine end to end: list what each side owns.

sessions.title: Complex Rook Endgames
sessions.concept: practical rook endgames
sessions.objective: Apply the practical principles of rook endgames.

sessions.title: Bishop vs Knight (Deep)
sessions.concept: deep bishop-versus-knight judgement
sessions.objective: Judge a bishop-versus-knight endgame from the pawn structure alone.

sessions.title: Queen & Pawn Endgames
sessions.concept: queen-and-pawn endgame technique
sessions.objective: Handle a queen-and-pawn endgame by applying one rule before calculating.

sessions.title: Fortresses & Theoretical Draws
sessions.concept: fortress
sessions.objective: Run the door test on a worse endgame — count what the stronger side needs, name which of the four doors his win must come through, shut it with one move, and say honestly when no door exists.

sessions.title: Endgame Technique Lab (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Advanced endgame technique starts with a judgement, not a move: name the ending, decide whether the position is one to convert or one to hold, and only then choose the move — because the converting move and the holding move are frequently different moves on the same board.
sessions.objective: Practise converting AND defending advanced endgames accurately in guided play: for each unlabelled position the student names the ending.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Advanced Endgames
sessions.concept: An advanced endgame is solved in one fixed order — name the ending, count what each side needs, state the verdict, then choose the move that verdict demands — and the review proves why the order matters: the same trade wins one card, strips a king on another and draws a third, so only the verdict distinguishes them.
sessions.objective: Solve mixed advanced-endgame problems: given an unlabelled position, the student names which of the unit's four endings is on the board.

sessions.title: Analyze Your Own Games (Deep)
sessions.concept: self-analysis method
sessions.objective: Analyse one of your own games deeply: put a price on every move, keep only the moves that cost more than half a pawn, sort those into four evidence-based types, name the cause behind each one, and turn the counts into a training plan.

sessions.title: Finding Critical Moments
sessions.concept: critical moment
sessions.objective: Find the moments that decided a finished game: write the verdict after every move using the one-and-a-half-pawn fence.

sessions.title: Using Engines Wisely
sessions.concept: engine as a checking tool
sessions.objective: Use an engine as a checking tool rather than a source of answers: measure a position at more than one depth.

sessions.title: Annotating a Game
sessions.concept: annotation
sessions.objective: Annotate a game so that every mark, every word and every variation is something the pupil can defend: award a symbol only when the evidence for it exists.

sessions.title: Group Analysis of a Classic
sessions.concept: group analysis
sessions.objective: Contribute ideas and variations in a guided group analysis of a classic game, and settle every suggestion with a verdict the room can check: a second road, a refutation with a line, or an honest parking space.

sessions.title: Build Your Study Plan (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: A study plan is honest when every slot is a measured weakness and the minutes follow the measurement: count your own priced mistakes, name each one, give the most minutes to the fault you make most often, and start the week with the fault that costs most each time.
sessions.objective: Create a concrete weekly study plan that targets measured weaknesses rather than guessed ones: the student takes the census of their own priced mistakes from the four games analysed in this unit.

sessions.title: Unit Review: The Art of Analysis
sessions.concept: The unit's five instruments are five different questions about the same move, and they do not agree: across the 70 free moves of one fresh game, S186 can name a fault on 8, S187 calls 3 critical, S188 has something to teach on 9, S189 permits a mark on 18 and S190 finds 51 crossroads — so the first move of any analysis is deciding which question you are asking.
sessions.objective: Apply the unit's five analysis instruments to a fresh game: given a position from a game the class has never analysed, the student states WHICH question is being asked, then answers it by that instrument's own rule.

sessions.title: Level 5A Checkpoint: The Analyst
sessions.concept: Sort the board before you solve it: assessment of deep strategy, advanced endgames and analysis
sessions.objective: Demonstrate Level 5A mastery across all three units of the level and earn The Analyst milestone.

sessions.title: Intuitive Sacrifices
sessions.concept: intuitive sacrifice
sessions.objective: Learn to judge a sacrifice that cannot be calculated to the end by naming its price first.

sessions.title: Creative Combinations from History
sessions.concept: Combination: a forced sequence whose end you can see before you start it
sessions.objective: Find the idea behind a famous creative combination by pricing what is handed over, proving the mate is forced against every defence, and naming which of the five ideas — DRAG, OPEN, VACATE, DEFLECT or BLOCK — is the one that makes the finish work.

sessions.title: Calculation vs Intuition
sessions.concept: forced mate as a proof rather than an opinion
sessions.objective: Decide between calculating and trusting your hand by testing every position for a short forced mate and counting the answers your opponent gets.

sessions.title: Risk Assessment in Complex Positions
sessions.concept: practical risk
sessions.objective: Assess practical risk in an unclear position by measuring two things — what the committal move gains over the quiet one, and how many follow-ups still keep it — and choose the sound, ambitious continuation on that basis.

sessions.title: Creative Play Challenges (Guided Practice)
sessions.concept: Creative play is not one skill but two, and the first move of every creative decision is choosing between them: if a forced finish exists the position is countable and calculation settles it completely, and if none exists the position can only be judged — by counting compensation against a bar, or by weighing what a bold move gains against how many good continuations survive it.
sessions.objective: Practise finding imaginative resources in challenge positions and games: for each unlabelled position the student first decides whether a forced finish is available to calculate or whether the position can only be judged.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Creative Chess
sessions.concept: Creative play is two instruments and one habit: if a forced finish exists the position is countable and only a proof will do, and if it does not then the resource can only be priced — so the first move of every creative decision is choosing the instrument, and this review proves the choice cannot be read off the difficulty, because every tier band contains both a countable card and a judgeable one.
sessions.objective: Solve creative problems where the engine-perfect path is non-obvious: given an unlabelled position.

sessions.title: Attacking Players
sessions.concept: the attacking style as a set of methods
sessions.objective: Describe the attacking style as five named methods, and apply one of them by counting the men who can reach the enemy king against the men guarding it before choosing between a blow and a preparation.

sessions.title: Positional Players
sessions.concept: the positional style as a set of methods
sessions.objective: Describe the positional style as five named methods, and apply one of them by taking the ledger of the four questions before deciding between a move that takes something and a move that spends nothing.

sessions.title: Universal Players
sessions.concept: the universal style
sessions.objective: Read the two free signals in front of the enemy king, pick the instrument the position is asking for, and switch instruments when the position changes.

sessions.title: Finding Your Style
sessions.concept: a playing style as a tie-breaker
sessions.objective: Price the two roads of a position against the engine's first choice.

sessions.title: A Game in Your Style (Model Game)
sessions.concept: a style read across a whole game
sessions.objective: Explain how a model game reflects a particular style.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Style & Identity
sessions.concept: A playing style is a preference exercised inside the board's limits, never a plan applied to every position: the board decides which instrument has jurisdiction and whether it says go or stop, and only when both roads sit inside the forty-centipawn band that makes two moves worth the same does the choice come back to the player — which is why this review can alternate attacking and positional answers card by card, put both inside every tier band, and answer five of its eight cards with a refusal.
sessions.objective: Match positions and plans to playing styles: given an unlabelled position.

sessions.title: Tournament Strategy
sessions.concept: tournament strategy
sessions.objective: Plan how to approach must-win, safe and recovery situations: count the slack your target leaves you, read what the position offers, and choose the road the scoreboard needs rather than the road the engine likes best.

sessions.title: Mental & Physical Preparation
sessions.concept: mental and physical preparation
sessions.objective: Students adopt three competition habits and see, in measured numbers from seven games this course has already analysed.

sessions.title: Building a Preparation File
sessions.concept: building a preparation file
sessions.objective: Students will begin a preparation file of their own.

sessions.title: Beyond the Curriculum — Self-Coaching
sessions.concept: self-coaching
sessions.objective: Route each of your own mistakes to the one kind of practice that repairs it, and set a long-term target whose horizon you have worked out rather than guessed.

sessions.title: Your Best Game (Game Review)
sessions.concept: Presenting your own best game: choose it with a five-test scorecard over the games you have actually analysed in full, then present it in 5 earned stops — turn, choice, plan, honest, finish — one of which must be your own worst move.
sessions.objective: Choose your best game with a scorecard instead of a feeling, then present it in 5 earned stops.

sessions.title: Unit Review: Competition & Path Forward
sessions.concept: Competition is chess with the world let back in: a standing, a body, a file, a record and an audience each get a vote that the position alone does not contain, and the discipline of Unit 6 is to name the voice, ask what it wants, and price it — which is why the same board can be a must-win and a safe board with two different right moves, why the only voice that asks you to give centipawns away on purpose asks for almost none of them, and why the review can put a 851-centipawn error on a Foundation card and a costless one on a Challenge card.
sessions.objective: Demonstrate competition planning and a personal study roadmap: given an unlabelled position, the student names which voice from outside the position has a vote.

sessions.title: Grand Capstone Review
sessions.concept: Interleaved review: sorting forcing from quiet before the search begins
sessions.objective: Pupils learn to sort a position before they search it: to ask whether something here is forcing, meaning it finishes the game or wins a piece by force, or whether nothing is forced and the right move simply makes the position better.

sessions.title: Queen Stage Final Assessment & Graduation
sessions.concept: Routing an unlabelled position to the right unit question, then answering it to graduate
sessions.objective: Demonstrate mastery of the whole Queen Stage by sitting an eight position paper whose seats are apportioned from the stage's own work, one for each of the six units and a second seat for the two units that carried the most material.
